issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s use of commercial premises for an additional or different trade does not constitute use for a purpose other than that for which the premises were let when the basic purpose remains trade and the letting contains no covenant restricting the tenant to a particular trade.
material_facts: The premises were let for the purpose of carrying on a trade, and there was no lease deed or covenant prohibiting the tenant from carrying on another trade.
The tenant continued selling shoes and also began selling ready-made garments.
The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the additional trade was a change of purpose.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s additional trade did not amount to use of the premises for a purpose other than that for which they were let, so eviction on this ground was not justified.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 10(2)(ii)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, change of use must be assessed in light of the terms of the letting, any restrictive covenant, and the nature of the tenancy. Section 21 of the Act and Section 108(o) of the Transfer of Property Act inform the inquiry. A change that makes the use alien to the purpose for which the premises were let may justify eviction, but a variation in the commodities sold does not do so where the basic activity remains trade and there is no covenant restricting other trades. The Court applied M.K. Palaniappa Chettiar v. A. Pennuswami Pillai, Mohan Lal v. Jai Bhagwan, Gurdial Batra v. Raj Kumar Jain, and Dashrath Baburao Sangale v. Kashimath Bhaskar Data; it distinguished M. Arul Jothi v. Lajja Bal because that case involved an express negative covenant, and also distinguished Ram Gopal v. Jai Narain because it concerned a change from commercial use to manufacturing.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and commercial_premises_leased_for_trade and no_covenant_limiting_trade and tenant_used_premises_for_another_trade and tenant_continued_original_trade

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant under rent-control law on the ground of change of use.
predicates.commercial_premises_leased_for_trade: The premises were let for the purpose of carrying on a trade.
predicates.no_covenant_limiting_trade: The letting contained no covenant restricting the tenant to a particular trade.
predicates.tenant_used_premises_for_another_trade: The tenant used the premises to carry on a trade in addition to or different from the trade initially carried on there.
predicates.tenant_continued_original_trade: The tenant continued the original trade while carrying on the additional or different trade.
predicates.change_of_user_eviction_unavailable: The tenant’s use does not justify eviction for change of purpose.

issues.definition: When commercial premises are let for trade without a covenant limiting the trade, and the tenant carries on another trade while continuing the original trade, the additional trade does not make eviction for change of purpose available.

issues.legal_issue: Trade-related fittings and alterations do not constitute actionable waste unless the evidence establishes that they are likely to materially impair the value or utility of the building.
material_facts: The tenant installed signboards and racks for the business, making holes in parts of the building, and obtained a separate electrical connection that also involved holes in the floor and walls.
The landlord alleged that these acts endangered or damaged the building and materially impaired its value or utility.
The engineer’s assertion that the parapet wall might collapse was unsupported by other evidence, and there was no adequate evidence of material impairment from the fittings or electrical work.
The landlord had permitted the tenant to put up boards.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not establish acts of waste likely to materially impair the building’s value or utility, so eviction on this ground was not justified.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(iii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 requires acts of waste likely to impair materially the value or utility of the building. The impairment need not be permanent, but it must be material; the alleged construction or alteration must substantially diminish the building’s value from a commercial, monetary, or utilitarian standpoint. The Court relied on G. Arunachalam v. Thondarperienambi, G. Raghunathan v. K.V. Varghese, and British Motor Car Co. v. Madan Lal Saggi, which discussed the material-impairment standard, including Om Prakash v. Amar Singh, Om Pal v. Anand Swarup, Waryam Singh v. Baldev Singh, Gurbachan Singh v. Shivalak Rubber Industries, and Vipin Kumar v. Roshan Lal Anand.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant under rent-control law on the ground of waste to the building.
predicates.tenant_made_trade_related_fittings_or_al: The tenant installed fittings or made alterations to the premises for the purpose of carrying on a trade.
predicates.no_material_impairment_proven: The evidence did not establish that the tenant’s acts were likely to materially impair the building’s value or utility.
predicates.waste_ground_eviction_unavailable: The tenant’s acts do not justify eviction for waste.

issues.definition: When a tenant makes trade-related fittings or alterations and material impairment of the building’s value or utility is not proven, eviction for waste is unavailable.
